title: Knight endings

D0.outcome: Explains why knight endings are slow and driven by the king: a knight needs up to six moves to cross the board, always changes square colour so it cannot lose a tempo, and stops a distant passed pawn only if it is already near.

D1.outcome: Counts knight routes between squares (four moves from a1 to b2, six from a1 to h8) and says which side's knight reaches the key square first in a simple ending with pawns.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled king, knight and pawn endings decides win, draw or plan: king first, the outside passed pawn, the knight to the pawn that cannot run; sees when the knight is too far to stop a rim pawn.

D3.outcome: Predicts the effect of one-feature changes (the extra pawn on the rim or not, one more move for the knight, the other side to move) and checks each prediction against the tablebase; uses knight parity to see who is in zugzwang.

misconceptions: A knight ending is a pawn ending with a knight added, so the knight needs no special care.
A knight can stop any passed pawn from anywhere on the board.
A knight can lose a tempo by a triangle, like a king.
A knight is always better than a bishop in endings with pawns.

conditions: Count the knight's journey, not the distance: it needs up to six moves between opposite corners and four between a1 and b2, and every move changes the colour of its square.

A passed pawn that engages both the enemy king and the enemy knight leaves only one defender for everything else, and a lone defending knight is too slow to hold a distant passer, so the defending king has to go.

An outside passed pawn wins a knight ending when the defender's king and knight cannot both stop it and still guard the pawns on the other wing; take the outside pawn away and the same ending can be a draw.
A lone knight stops a rim pawn only if it is already near the pawn's path: on the rim it has at most four moves and in the corner two, so a knight on the far side of the board arrives too late.
Because a knight changes square colour with every move, it cannot lose a tempo by itself the way a king or a bishop can; where the move decides, count the parity (END.TEMPO).

contrasts: The extra pawn stands on the same wing as the others, so there is no outside passer and the ending is a draw.
The knight is one move too far from the rim pawn's path: it looks close, but the pawn queens.
A bishop instead of the knight, or a rook ending: the bishop covers both wings from afar, so the knight's slowness rules do not carry over (END.MINOR).
